turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Brennan, in you come. I'll grab a blood pressure before the doctor sees you. 136 over 84, pulse 58, and the scales have you at 89 kilos.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's grand. Sit yourselves down. What has you in?

[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): The tiredness, doctor, though if I start properly I'll wander. I do the accounts at the co-op, the month-end is a killer, I'm 53 in March, and I've been putting the whole lot down to the job and to getting older.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's asleep in the armchair before the nine o'clock news, most nights. I had to drag him in.

[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I was getting to that. I couldn't tell you when the tiredness began — last winter, or the one before, one or the other. I'm no use after half four, and the backlog at work just sits there.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the fatigue's been there a good while, and you can't pin the start. Are you cold with it as well?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Freezing, even with the heating up and a jumper on in the kitchen. That's been the same stretch of time, whatever length it is, hands worst of all, and the weight —
[SEG0008] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry — the jumper is year-round. He had it on in June.

[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): The weight, yes. You've me at 89. I was twelve stone a few years back, about 76 kilos, so that's the best part of two stone, and I haven't really changed the eating, only more tea and biscuits at the desk because the days run long.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight up, cold, tired. What about the bowels, any change? And has your mood dipped, or is it just the energy?

[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): The bowels are a misery. Constipated, every three or four days, hard stools, and I'm after trying prunes and then senna from the chemist. The mood I'll come to, because the senna is a small saga in itself —
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much senna, and how long have you been on it?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Two tablets at night, only the last fortnight, and it's done nothing. I read the packet twice so I wouldn't take the wrong amount, and I still feel blocked.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been very flat as well, and the garden's gone to —

[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the mood you asked about. I'm low. No interest in the garden and I used to live out there. I don't think I'm depressed, I just put the flatness down to being wrecked from work.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Low, but not depression in your own view. Any thyroid trouble in the family?
[SEG0017] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His mother had the underactive thyroid, for years.

[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Eltroxin, they called the tablets, right up until she died, God rest her. I think her sister might have had something similar but I never got that straight, so I won't swear to it. I had a blood test myself once and they told me it was borderline.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was that blood test?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): I couldn't date it if you paid me. Before the pandemic, or just after, or somewhere in between. They said borderline, I'm nearly sure of the word.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The letter said normal, Seán. It's in the sideboard at home. You've called it borderline for years and it wasn't.
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Was it normal? I was certain they said borderline. Sure maybe I have it wrong — I do mix the old results up.

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, we won't hang anything on that old result, since you remember borderline and your wife remembers a normal letter, and neither of you can date it. Let me say back what I have. Tired and cold since last winter or the winter before, weight from about 76 kilos up to 89, bowels every three or four days, mood low but not what you'd call depression, mother with an underactive thyroid, senna two at night for a fortnight with no joy.
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the bones of it. I still think the co-op hours are half the story, mind you, and the age.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): They might well be. On examination your hands are cool, the pulse matches the 58 the nurse got, and I can't feel any enlargement or lump in the thyroid itself.
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): Is a normal feel a good thing? My mother had a goitre late on — or was that someone else. No, it was her, I'm sure of that much.

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): A normal feel doesn't rule an underactive thyroid in or out. This could be hypothyroidism, or it could be the workload and age catching you, and I can't tell those apart from the chair.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So you'll do a blood test, will you?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I will. I'll order a thyroid function test, and a full blood count as well, with the tiredness gone on this long. Not this minute — the nurse will book the phlebotomy.
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday morning is free, if that suits ye. I can put the form through now.

[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Thursday morning is the audit, I can't do morning, the regional manager is in and I'll be stuck at the desk till lunch. Afternoon I could manage, if there's a slot, though the car park is desperate after three —
[SEG0032] person_1 (NURSE): Afternoon, so. Half two.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. Leave the senna off, since two at night for a fortnight hasn't shifted things. Plenty of water, and don't write the whole thing off as age until we have the numbers.

[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): If it is the thyroid, is it the same tablet my mother was on? I don't fancy being on something for life if I can avoid it, though I know people are, and she managed grand on it for years.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): We don't start any tablet until the result is back, and we'll talk it through then. Come back to me about a week after Thursday, once the results are in.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll root out that old letter so you're not depending on his memory of it.
